Before waxing, you should know there are two types of waxes: hard and soft.

According to recent reports, if you want to use something stripless, go for hard wax. It adheres to the hair follicle (versus the skin), hardens, and can be removed on its own, eliminating the need for paper strips. For some, it may even feel less painful than soft wax, so it's great for sensitive skin, claims dermatologist Nazanin Saedi, MD. The only caveat is that you may have to apply it several times in the same area to make sure all the hairs you target are removed.

It has been revealed that soft wax, on the other hand, is soft and applied in a thin layer. A paper strip is then used to adhere and remove the wax. Often, the top layer of skin is also removed, so it can be irritating for people with sensitive skin.

Ideally, beginners should look for kits that contain everything they need to get the job done—wax, strips, and finishing oil, at minimum. Novices may also appreciate waxing kits that come with pre-loaded strips, since they're less messy and require less precision. The tradeoff? You're limited to the size of the included strips, so look for kits with multiple sizes if you're targeting different areas of the body. Larger strips are fantastic for your legs, while small strips are practical for your face.

Sources indicate that it's crucial to use the safest and gentlest wax kits available to avoid irritating, burning, and potentially scarring your skin. If you have sensitive skin, look for waxing kits that include skin-soothing ingredients, like castor and almond oils or aloe. And whatever you use, first test the wax in an area on your body that isn't too visible. This will allow you to see if it is gentle enough for your skin. If you experience a bad reaction, you'll know it's time to pivot to a different product.

It has been revealed that for the past year, Women’s Health contributors and I, including Sabrina Talbert, Jasmine Gomez, Danielle Jackson, and Cristina Montemayor, tested the bestselling, most popular, and top-rated at-home waxing kits. Our team consulted dermatologists Blair Murphy-Rose, MD, Nazanin Saedi, MD, and Uchenna Okereke, MD, for pre-waxing advice and aftercare instructions to prevent irritation and promote healthy skin. Then, we got our hands on the kits and tested them in the comfort of our own homes, evaluating attributes like ease of use, comfort, results, and overall value. Of the 25 at-home waxing kits tested, the seven on this list delivered the best results in our in-depth evaluations.

At-home waxing removes body hair conveniently and cost-effectively, and the best kits do it quickly while minimizing pain and irritation. So, if you’re ready to ditch the razors, check out this list of the best waxing kits, tested by dermatologists and WH editors.

After waxing, you can prevent ingrown hairs from forming and minimize irritation immediately afterward by applying cool aloe to soothe skin, and sticking to loose clothes that won't create friction. "Aloe vera has anti-inflammatory properties that help soothe sunburned skin, while glycerin specifically can help to boost hydration levels to restore the skin's moisture barrier," dermatologist Divya Shokeen, MD, previously told WH in our guide to the best aloe vera gel. Some kits also come with nourishing oils and wipes to help minimize any post-wax irritation.

Before you head off to wax unwanted hair, these are a few other tips you should keep in mind.

Waxing removes hair by lifting it out at the root. With traditional waxing, hot wax is applied to skin and the hair is pulled off in the opposite direction of the way it's growing. The key word here and what can make at-home waxing dangerous is that it's hot.

Recent findings suggest that “Hot wax can burn the skin—and it is a particularly dangerous type of burn because the hot product adheres to the skin,” says Dr. Murphy-Rose. Always make sure you're following the heating directions closely and that you hold your hand over the wax after it's been heated to gauge the temperature before applying it to your skin.

It has been revealed that then, first test the wax in an area on your body that isn't too visible. "That way you can check the temperature, but also see how your skin reacts," says Dr. Saedi. Testing a product will also allow you to see if it is gentle enough for your skin. “It's key to use the safest and gentlest wax kits available to avoid irritating, burning, and potentially scarring your skin," says Dr. Murphy-Rose. You should also avoid any ingredients you have a known allergy or sensitivity to. If you experience a bad reaction, you'll know it's time to pivot to a different product.

Sources indicate that "Hot wax tends to adhere the strongest, so while it may remove hairs more efficiently, it can also stick to skin more and pull off those top layers of the skin as it's also pulling out your hair,” claims Dr. Murphy-Rose.

Waxing exfoliates the top layer of skin and is more likely to cause hyperpigmentation a.k.a. dark spots, indicates Dr. Okereke. She says to think of the skin after waxing like a fresh, pink wound. "Ultraviolet rays are attracted to wounds, making the freshly waxed skin more susceptible to darkening as melanin (the dark pigment in skin) floods the area to try and protect it." Luckily, there is a simple fix: Wear broad-spectrum sunscreen! Better yet, keep that new skin out of the sun completely for at least a few days.

You'll also want to avoid any extra exfoliation, like retinol, chemical peels, and microdermabrasion, a few days prior and a few days following your at-home wax. A few other good things to know before getting started: Always wax on clean skin to avoid bacterial contamination in pores and make sure your hairs are long enough (at least 1/4 of an inch) to be grabbed by the wax.

Sources indicate that the key to preventing ingrown hairs (an all too common downside of waxing for many) is to get the full hair follicle. The best way to do this is by keeping your skin taut and pulling the wax strip in the opposite direction of the way that your hair grows.

In a recent development, sugaring, aka sugared wax or sugar gel, is generally safer because it’s applied to skin at room temperature (read: no risk of burning skin) and warms up with body heat. “Sugared ‘wax’ is not truly wax,” Dr. Murphy-Rose says. Rather, it’s a combination of sugar, lemon juice, and water. Some brands will infuse glycerin, fragrance, honey, or essential oils. Regardless of which brand you opt for, sugaring is water-soluble and easily rinses off the skin compared to hot wax, she says.

Recent findings suggest that sugaring and threading remove the hair follicle from the root but with less exfoliating, offering a gentler process, Dr. Okereke says. Though she warns that she's also had patients with coily-textured hair that still develop ingrown hairs and scarring from sugaring as well. The bottom line: "If you know you're prone to hyperpigmentation, ingrown hairs, or scarring, see a dermatologist to discuss the best hair removal practices for you," says Dr. Okereke.

Sources indicate that few artisanal traditions are so linked with a place that its geographical namesake winds up in the global lexicon. In the case of fine wool shawls from Kashmir—prized among 19th-century Europeans, including Joséphine Bonaparte—the word cashmere stuck. For Kadri Mujtaba, a fascination with these textiles came early. Born into a family of merchants and weavers in the region’s city of Srinagar, he observed a deep-rooted culture around hand-spun yarn and small wooden looms.

A bouquet of lotus pods held up against the brand’s Mountain blanket in pine.

One of the studio’s handmade shawl looms.

A Doorway Sozni twill blanket draped over a chair.

“It’s the original work-from-home idea,” he says of the technique, passed down for centuries. Amid encroaching mechanization, Mujtaba has stayed committed to slow craft, cultivating a network of some 2,000 artisans over the past two decades. Initially he’d create custom pieces for designers and brands (Pierre Yovanovitch, The Row, Luis Laplace) and host high-end trunk indicates. That is how Jonathan Renker—via his father, a longtime customer—first encountered the wares. Now, he and Mujtaba have partnered on Kadri: a new brand of cashmere accessories and home goods that marry Kashmiri refinement and streamlined design.

A Jaali Kaani blanket on the grounds of Pari Mahal garden.

A wood swift of cashmere yarn at the Kadri atelier.

Shawls and scarves from Kadri’s debut collection.

Sources indicate that the firm debuts with a collection of scarves, throws, and blankets. The cofounders enlisted creative director Dan Thawley and textile designer Maeva Elfassi, who distilled the Kashmir Valley landscape into shades of tobacco, lime, vermilion, and—as a nod to Srinagar’s Dal Lake—dusty blue. Wool from Changthangi goats, which graze across the plateaus of nearby Ladakh, is spun by hand, resulting in airy, ultrasoft knits. More impressive still is the subtlety on display. A bouclé piece has the immersive pull of a Color Field painting, while a quilted scarf joins two paper-thin layers. Just one blanket requires months of work and a balletic dance of bobbins.

Sources indicate that “What makes Kadri so special is this research-and-development approach,” says Renker, describing a push toward novel applications while holding fast to the handmade vernacular. “The only electricity that’s used are the overhead lights on a cloudy day.”.

Industry observers note that I REMEMBER THE first time I became aware of it. Or should I say lack of it.

According to recent reports, I grew up in the mid '80s. A magical time. MTV actually played music videos. New Coke was a thing people cared about. And a ginger-headed German teenager named Boris Becker—Boom-Boom, to his millions of fans—became, at age 17, the youngest player ever to win Wimbledon.

I was nine years old. And obsessed.

According to recent reports, while other kids my age were collecting Garbage Pail Kids cards or trying to solve Rubik’s Cubes, I was rewatching VHS recordings of Becker’s matches. I practiced his signature serve motion in front of my bedroom mirror. I begged—actually begged—my parents for the complete Boris Becker starter kit: the Ellesse tennis outfit, the Puma half-top sneakers, and the holy grail itself: the Puma Super tennis racket.

According to recent reports, the problem was, no matter how hard I tried, no matter how much Hi-C I consumed, I could never quite achieve the same explosive spring that made Boom-Boom so spectacular. Then I noticed something about Becker’s serve—the one that earned him his nickname. Most players bent their knees to generate power. Becker did something else.

He stuck out his butt. Like, really stuck it out. His serve motion involved this pronounced posterior thrust that helped him achieve that devastating topspin and pace.

In a recent development, I went to the bedroom mirror. Turned sideways. Attempted the same motion. And that’s when it hit me with all the force of one of Becker’s 130-mph serves: I didn’t have a butt to stick out. Where Becker had curvature, I had...continuity. My back just sort of continued into my legs.

Reality set in. No bum-bum, no boom-boom.

By high school, I had pivoted to more cerebral pursuits like creative writing and a burgeoning interest in art history. Art history seemed safe—just looking at old paintings and Roman sculptures, right? Wrong. It became immediately clear that every civilization in human history had one thing in common: great asses.

One fateful morning during my sophomore year, I was standing at my locker wearing a pair of saggy-bottomed Gap khakis when I heard giggles behind me. The distinctive sound of teenage girls discovering something hilarious and vaguely cruel.

“Oh my God,” one of them mentioned. I froze.

“He has no butt!” another voice confirmed with the confidence of a scientist making a groundbreaking discovery. More giggling. Then came the death blow that would echo through the halls of my high school for the next two and a half years:.

Sure, it wasn’t the most creative nickname, but it had just enough alliteration to spread like a pre-internet meme. From that day on, I knew “they” knew.

In a recent development, I RECENTLY TURNED 50. I’m happily married and have two amazing kids. Life is good, but I’d be lying if I said the ghost of No-Butt Bender doesn’t haunt me. As I’ve aged, what little I had has somehow continued to erode. My wife loves me despite my anatomical deficiency but remains perpetually baffled by the lack of rear topography. And what was once giggles from teenage girls is now full-throated hysterical laughter from my 13- and 11-year-old children when they catch a glimpse of me in anything form-fitting.

Recently, Instagram’s insecurity algorithm served me up an ad for Perk men’s clothing. Their website is a gallery of flattering middle-aged bum-shots, but what really stopped my scroll was the pitch for their pants: “Our chinos magically turn even a flat butt into a compliment magnet. Whether you’re 25 or 65, that never gets old!”.

You have to understand—when you have no butt, no pants are flattering. So when Perk starts advertising pants that promise to be so bootylicious you’ll receive compliments everywhere you go, I dared to dream. I did what any man starved for posterior validation does—panic-ordered chinos in every damn color.

In a recent development, five pairs. Overnight shipping.

Sources indicate that the moment the package arrived, I tore it open. I slipped them on, turned toward the mirror, and—holy hell—was that…something? An actual curve? A protrusion? I squinted. I turned. And I practically sprinted to the living room where the family was waiting and struck a pose.

It has been revealed that crickets. Then a full collapse into hysterical laughter.

“I’m sorry,” my wife gasped between laughs, “but those pants are working so hard and getting nowhere.”.

I was tired of feeling like the only person other than Hank Hill to be cursed with diminished gluteal syndrome (DGS). It’s a very isolating condition. But I figured if Perk could build an entire organization around flat-figured men, there had to be others out there, living their lives in quiet resignation.

Close to midnight on a Wednesday, my face lit only by the glow of my computer, I did the obvious: Googled “men with no butts.”.

Industry observers note that the search results led me to a Reddit post titled, “Gentlemen, how do you live with having no butt?” This guy laid it all out: approaching 29, finally accepting his glute-free reality, enduring constant jokes from his girlfriend, the whole nine yards of tush-less trauma. But what really got me was his closing line: “Please help.”.

I stared at those two words. They contained decades of my own experience—the loneliness, the confusion, the desperation. This post was five years old, but I didn’t care. I had to reach out.

I woke the following morning to find his response waiting like a message from a long-lost brother: “You seem legit I guess. Sure why not.” We were already bonding!

I asked Ross (names have been changed to protect the in-ass-cent) what motivated him to publicly post about his crisis on Reddit, and he mentioned, “It was a genuine problem and if someone’s got an answer that helps, I was going to be all ears.”.

Industry observers note that ross first became aware of his DGS when a friend at the gym dropped the bomb: “Dude, you have no ass whatsoever.” The keen observation sent Ross into a spiral of photographic evidence review. He started examining pictures of himself and came to the only possible conclusion: “Huh, I guess I don’t.” It was his own bedroom-mirror moment.

Industry observers note that as for the wisdom he received from the Reddit hivemind, he remarked it was mostly people prescribing the usual suspects: sprints and squats: “I was doing a shit ton of those back then and still do,” he told me. Five years later, he reports modest gains: “It’s no dump truck but I’ve got a little bit of cushion for comfort back there.” He eventually broke up with the ass-teaser (good riddance) and has been dating a new lady who actually pinches it every now and then—a gesture that, for men like us, feels like winning the Mega Millions.

It has been revealed that but the struggle continues. Despite his Stairmaster devotion, sweatpants still “kind of sag” making it look like he may have taken a small dump in them. Still, Ross gave me the faintest glimmer that improvement was possible. Maybe a guy with no butt could transform it into a bona fide ba-donk-a-donk.

I phoned two lifelines from my past—Jonathan Botts, MD, a college friend who’d become an orthopedic surgeon at the Los Angeles Orthopedic Institute in Sherman Oaks, California, and Derek DeGrazio, Britney Spears’s former physical trainer, who had whipped me into the best shape of my life for my long-ago wedding and now is a partner at Barry’s Bootcamp Miami.

Dr. Botts (who inexplicably escaped high school without a single butt-related nickname) broke down the anatomy: the butt consists of three muscles—the gluteus maximus, medius, and minimus—but it’s the maximus that does the heavy lifting in filling out a man’s pants.

When I asked about the possibility of maximizing my non-existus, he didn’t sugarcoat it. “Here’s the problem: You can’t go from what you are now to just working on your butt and developing a huge butt,” he told me. “People are doing lots of protein intake and protein shakes and bulking up like that. You could get bigger and your butt would get bigger with you. Muscularly. But I don’t know. I don’t think you could take huge leaps with just doing squats and lunges.”.

So basically, I’d need to become the Hulk to grow a butt.

According to recent reports, derek offered an alternate strategy with what he calls the Bender Significant Three™. “I can’t say for certain, but I think No-Butt Bender can become Mild-Butt Bender with squats for foundation, Romanian deadlifts to pop your glute a little bit, and a nice hip thrust,” he noted.

Mild-Butt Bender. It did have a certain je ne sais quoi.

Derek, who freely admits he was born with “a great Italian ass,” is my gluteal bizarro from an alternate universe where only perfect butts exist. He told me his seat meat gave him confidence in high school, something I could only imagine by taping Springsteen’s Born in the USA album cover to the back of my pants. Derek played baseball, a sport notorious for its revealing tight pants. “I don’t know if they came to watch baseball or if they came to watch us in our uniforms,” he recalled, misty-eyed.

In a recent development, I hated him. I loved him. I wanted to be him.

Sources indicate that but then—plot twist!—just as I began fantasizing about playing shortstop, Derek dropped a bomb: “I started to realize that what was a blessing at one point became also my Achilles heel at the same time. If there is a downside, I wasn’t the fastest guy on the team.”.

Industry observers note that wait. There was a downside to having a butt?

It has been revealed that dr. Botts, who describes his own posterior as “bigger than average,” delivered the final revelation: Having a bigger butt doesn’t automatically mean you have a stronger butt. “If you have a small butt, does that mean you have weak glutes? It doesn’t at all. You can have a substantial butt and have really weak glutes.”.

All these years, I’d associated my small butt with weakness. With inadequacy. With being less than. What if I was wrong? What if, beneath my perpetually drooping pants lurked a superhero-strength posterior more powerful than even Derek’s celebrated Italian ass?

Industry observers note that unlikely. And who am I kidding? It’s not like if I had said to those girls in high school, “Oh no, you don’t understand—it’s really strong!” they would have stopped laughing and made out with me.

Industry observers note that but hey, this newly introduced knowledge gives me something to cling on to. Wish I could say the same for my pants. Still, I am what I am. I am No-Butt Bender. And if that makes my kids laugh and my wife give me a warm, “It’s okay. I love you anyway” hug, I’ll take it.

First posed by Bernhard Riemann in 1859, the hypothesis predicts where certain zeros of the Riemann zeta function fall. The question matters because those zeros are linked to the distribution of prime numbers, whose patterns underlie extensive mathematical research.

A proof would be a historic mathematical result, since experts have been trying to solve that for over a century.

Industry observers note that lean can verify that formal deductions obey its rules. Mathematicians still need to reproduce the archive, check the formalized theorem matches the original conjecture, and examine the claimed result before considering it settled.

Under the institute’s prize rules, a proposed solution must be published in a qualifying outlet, survive at least two years of scrutiny, and earn general acceptance before the prize can be considered.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After delaying development of the long-awaited electric Golf, Volkswagen is delaying another EV based on its SSP platform.

As it scrambles to cut costs, Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer revealed in an internal memo at the end of October that development of the all-electric Golf is being delayed at its Wolfsburg plant in Germany.

The news comes after the VW Group posted an operating loss of €5.9 billion ($6.5 billion) in the third quarter, its largest quarterly loss since the infamous Dieselgate scandal in 2015.

“We simply can’t afford this work right now,” Schäfer said in the memo reviewed by Reuters. The Wolfsburg plant, AKA the “heart of the VW brand,” is about €300 million ($334.5 million) short of its cost-cutting targets, the memo said.

Volkswagen initially planned to launch the Golf EV in 2028, but Schäfer announced earlier this year that the long-awaited electric car was delayed until closer to 2030.

Schäfer suggested the delay was because the SSP (Scalable Systems Platform), which is being developed through its partnership with Rivian, was taking longer than expected, again due to costs.

According to Autocar, Volkswagen is now delaying the Audi A4 E-tron as well, another vehicle that was initially planned to be among the first based on the SSP platform.

In a recent development, production of the electric A4 is being pushed back until at least 2029, a year later than originally planned. While the delay is disappointing for Audi fans (including myself) still waiting for an electric A4, it also puts Audi behind rival luxury brands in the mid-size sedan segment.

BMW has the newly introduced i3, and Mercedes-Benz has the C-Class EV, both of which feature major improvements in range, charging, and efficiency over their previous-generation EVs.

Volkswagen remarked in 2023 that the 800V SSP will serve as a “single future backbone with integrated electric and electronics architecture,” claiming that more than 40 million models were expected to be built on it.

The manufacturer also stated investment and R&D costs were expected to be reduced by about 30% compared to the current MEB platform, enabling most models “to achieve the same margin compared to their conventionally powered counterparts.”.

Volkswagen’s software struggles started in its internal division, Cariad, leading to delays, missed targets, and budget overruns.

To fix it, VW turned to Rivian, forming a joint venture to develop its next-gen software-defined vehicle (SDV) electrical architecture.

In March, VW noted several test vehicles, including the ID.EVERY1, Audi, and Scout with the SDV architecture underwent “comprehensive evaluation,” and successfully validated over-the-air (OTA) functionality.

Being cash efficient is good, but delays to the next-gen platform that will keep you competitive with rival brands seem like a problem.

However, the Audi A4 E-tron delay is not entirely about software. The Autocar report claims Audi demanded significant changes to the SSP platform for the A4 E-tron so it more closely matched the current gas version.

Audi reportedly wanted individual footwells for front and rear passengers, which would require repositioning the battery.

The luxury brand also reportedly asked for a 48V electrical system instead of the traditional 12V setup initially planned.

Industry observers note that while development of the Golf EV is on hold, VW’s works council noted the pause will not delay its launch, promising to make up for lost time. It’s still expected to launch in 2030. The Audi A4 E-tron is now expected to arrive around 2029.

It’s easy to underrate walking as one of the best things we can do for our fitness—after all, it doesn’t get your heart rate up like running or a HIIT workout. But that doesn’t mean you’re not getting tons of physical and mental health benefits from walking, whether you’re following a walking workout plan or not.

According to recent reports, and perhaps one of the best things about walking is that it doesn’t require any specialized equipment or gear except a really good pair of comfy walking shoes. Luckily for you, we’re constantly testing walking shoes, and we’ve narrowed down all the options out there to a list of pairs we reach for again and again. We’ve used our testing experience, plus picked the brains of podiatrists and other experts to compile our favorites in this guide.

If you’ve logged even a couple of miles in a not-so-great pair of walking shoes, you know wearing the wrong footwear can make what started out as a nice walk turn into an uncomfortable slog fast (we’re talking blisters, achy arches, plantar fasciitis, and more).

Recent findings suggest that the right walking shoes, on the other hand, can help you walk farther, feel happier while doing it, and gush to friends about your sneakers (ask us how we know). Plus, select styles can help prevent injury or overpronation (when your arches collapse and cause your foot to angle inward), states podiatrist Chanel Perkins, DPM, an assistant professor of foot and ankle podiatry in the Department of Orthopedic Surgery and Rehabilitation at the University of Texas Medical Branch.

It has been revealed that after testing dozens of walking shoes for our 2026 Fitness Awards, the Adrenaline GTS 25 took the top spot for its near-perfect balance between cushioning and stability. Our staffers who tested it say it’s comfortable enough to walk in for hours. “It offers just the right amount of cushioning for a bouncy step without compromising on support for my flat, wide feet,” says WH beauty editor Nicole Saunders.

That comfort starts with the 25’s updated midsole, which feels plusher than previous models without losing an ounce of stability. It still features the brand’s signature GuardRails technology—firmer along the sides and softer through the center—to gently lock in your stride. In our testing, Brooks continues to set the standard for stability, making this a standout pick for anyone whose feet tend to roll inward while walking.

Industry observers note that when it comes to fit, the 25 has a roomier toe box up front and a secure (but still comfortable) heel lock back, which helps cut down on friction and lowers your chances of blisters during long walks. The higher 10 mm drop creates a slightly forward-leaning stride that takes pressure off the calves and Achilles, making the 25 a smart pick for anyone with tight lower legs or Achilles sensitivity. If you prefer a flatter feel underfoot, though, we recommend something lower profile like the Hoka Mach 6.

At 9.5 ounces, it’s one of the heavier options on this list, but that added weight comes from the stability tech and structured testing. We barely noticed the difference, especially once we got moving.

Read More: Best Brooks Shoes for Walking.

Diana Rogers, DPM, a podiatric foot and ankle surgery specialist in Crystal Lake, Illinois, and Casey Pidich, MD, a podiatrist and foot and ankle surgeon based in the Bronx, New York, both recommend Hoka’s Clifton series to patients for arch support, so you know it's a good one.

According to recent reports, pidich loves that the design encourages great form—the sole ensures that your feet rock off the ground rather than push off your toes. Rogers specifically recommends the shoe for her plantar fasciitis (a condition where you feel pain in the arch) patients for this exact reason. “The lightweight feel on this shoe propels feet forward rather than making them do extra work,” she claims.

WH style editor Shannon Zitz found in her testing that the foam absorbed impact well on both pavement and the treadmill. “My feet—unfortunately plagued by plantar fasciitis—never felt fatigued wearing this shoe,” she said, noting that her stride felt smooth and natural.

The Clifton 11 is available in wide and extra-wide sizing, making it a good fit for a wide variety of walkers.

According to recent reports, for those who appreciate a good slip-on shoe, the Skechers Go Walk Flex Azriel’s lightweight, breathable mesh upper is great for sweaty feet, while hovering around a bargain price of about $60 (and on sale for cheaper sometimes). The ultra-cushioned midsole offers great arch support, too.

“This is a solid no-frills walking shoe that’s perfect for errands, quick hot girl strolls, or for walking your dog,” claims WH style editor Shannen Zitz. “I love that it slips on easily while still having the appearance of a classic sneaker with bungee laces that never come undone.”.

Zitz was skeptical about whether the slip-on would be supportive and secure enough, but the breathable, stretchy mesh offered surprisingly good compression around her feet.

“It keeps my feet locked in and has never caused any pain or blisters,” she says. “While I wouldn’t log miles in this shoe, it is cushioned and supportive enough for long periods of standing or casual wear.” However, she finds the style a bit orthopedic-looking, although the white colorway can look cute with jeans or dresses.

Read More: Best Skechers For Walking.

Asics is considered a classic, all-around great brand for walking, especially if you struggle with overpronation (ankles that roll inward) or have flat feet. Take the Gel-Kayano 32, which has thick foam borders on each side to encourage proper alignment and walking gait. Deep heel cups also help keep arches supported—there’s a reason this shoe made our best plantar fasciitis walking shoe guide.

It has been revealed that fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi is a huge fan of the firm, stiffer midsole that still maintains massive plushness with its signature gel cushioning system for superior shock absorption. “My landings feel like I’m hovering above ground, which states a lot given I stomp on hard pavement daily. I actually find it more cushioned than the Hoka Mach 6,” she says. The heel-to-toe drop is 8 millimeters, which Accardi says is a bit high for her liking, but ideal if you want to take all the pressure away from your arches.

Sources indicate that the Hoka Mach 7 is Zitz’s personal favorite. While it’s technically a running shoe, she loves it for recovery and walking. “I’ve been living in this sneaker since returning from a week-long hiking trip where I logged about 20K steps per day,” she says. “It’s flexible, lightweight, and cushioned—it basically feels like a hug for my super tired feet.” The cushioning also doesn’t feel bulky compared to other Hoka models, such as the Bondi 8.

The previous iteration, the Mach 6, took home our 2025 Fitness Award for top walking shoe thanks to its blend of responsive cushioning, breathability, and lightweight construction—and the Mach 7 has built on that winning formula with an updated outer and grippier bottom. Zitz tested this shoe after it first dropped, walking more than 150 miles in it—and not once did she feel even a bit of foot fatigue or soreness.

Another brownie point? It comes in wide sizing. Some WH editors find standard Hoka sizing pretty narrow, but the wide fit has adequate space in the toe box, so you can walk for hours without experiencing any friction. For extra room overall, podiatrist Shital Sharma, DPM, a podiatrist at Pinewood Family Care Co. in New Jersey, recommends going up a half-size in all walking sneakers because your feet tend to swell and expand from physical activity.

Lined with mesh to make this an ultra-breathable sneaker, the Pegasus is a winner because it has a slim, low heel that Perkins says is awesome for maintaining a smooth walking cadence. We love that the 42 is lighter than the previous model and has a curvier toe box that gives more toe spring, a smoother ride, and a roomier fit.

According to recent reports, WH Fitness Director Jacqueline Andriakos has worn countless versions of the Nike Pegasus for both running and walking and has logged hundreds of miles in it. “I find the sole a bit on the firmer side, and the mesh upper really hugs and forms to your individual foot shape,” she says. “The shoe feels perfectly snug and secure as you step without being too constricting.”.

She does flag that the tongue sometimes gets folded up and tucked under the laces in a slightly uncomfortable way. “I fix this by being really diligent when I put the shoes on, making sure to pull the tongue taut and make sure it's lying flat before tying my shoes.”.

Sources indicate that the shoe is super breathable and lightweight, which makes it a great option for spring and summer, but less so for cold or wet weather. Overall, this is Andriakos’ go-to walking shoe recommendation for her friends and family—and so far she's only heard happy feedback from loved ones who have purchased a Pegasus shoe.

The latest edition of the Fresh Foam X 1080 wows us with its inclusive sizing, with narrow, standard, wide, and extra-wide fits available to accommodate all feet.

In a recent development, “I have a hard time finding walking shoes that are both cushioned and supportive enough for my high arches and sensitive balls of the feet, but that are also narrow enough,” Andriakos indicates. “This is absolutely perfect if you deal with any foot pain concerns or struggle with sneakers being a bit too wide—I have walked over 100 miles in these at this point and have never even had a sore or tender spot from rubbing or chafing (they also required zero break-in period).”Andriakos also finds the laces are very secure and don’t come untied easily. The only downside? “When I’ve worn it on rainy days, I notice my feet will feel damp and it takes a bit to dry out.” To help combat that, she just throws it in the dryer (which, to be clear, isn’t recommended by the brand, but she found it hasn't damaged the silhouette!).

Read More: Best New Balance Shoes.

In a recent development, the On Cloudtilt Remix is built for walking, thanks to its sequence of collapsing “cloud” foam to deliver a smooth, plush ride. It has maximum cushioning and bounce, compared to lots of other walking shoes we’ve tested, making it a solid pick for walkers and casual runners who prefer a softer, cushier feel underfoot.

In a recent development, zitz recently added this pair to her collection and appreciates how lightweight and springy it feels. “I feel like I have such a pep in my step when I wear it—which is basically all the time since it’s so stylish,” she says. “I love the layers of see-through mesh on the upper, which looks super modern and clean. I’ve been wearing this shoe nonstop with capris, leggings, and athletic shorts.”.

Sources indicate that this style features Helion Superfoam (a blend of firm and flexible foam components) that delivers bounce without a lot of bulk. It also has a moderate 7 mm heel-to-toe drop, meaning it distributes weight evenly throughout the lower body, making it a pretty good pick for most walkers. It’s the perfect shoe that combines all our must-have walking shoe features into one sleek kick.

The Latest Balance 608 V5 Trainer has over 38,000 reviews on Amazon, and for good reason. The brand integrated its signature ABZORB midsole (a blend of substantial foam cushioning with compression resistance), which is designed to lessen the blow on joints when walking.

The 608 has tons of shock absorption which makes it great for neutral to high arches. But since it lacks stability features, it’s not our top choice for flat feet. We do like that it comes in narrow, standard, and wide sizing.

It has been revealed that ideally, walking shoes will assist with your gait (your walking pattern) instead of just cushioning impact. Your shoe should also be somewhat stiff—the more it bends, the less stability it will have.

To test the flexibility, hold the shoe at the toe box and heel counter and try to fold the shoe in half by pushing on its ends to see how sturdy it is. If it folds in half or twists with ease, it’s too flexible, indicates podiatrist Elizabeth Daughtry, MD, a podiatrist and foot and ankle specialist with Foot and Ankle Specialists of the Mid-Atlantic in Cary, North Carolina.

She also adds that seeking out a shoe with a boat-like (rockered) shape, rigid midsole, and firm heel counter can help stabilize feet, control overpronation (collapsing arches), and prevent heel striking.

Industry observers note that look for walking shoes that have an outsole with more rigidity in the midsole for stability. Different feet have different needs, so it’s vital to have insoles that can be removed in case you use orthotics. “Most shoes don’t offer adequate support alone,” notes Dr. Daughtry. “You should supplement most shoes with a more custom-molded orthotic, which your local podiatrist can make for you, as this provides adequate support and helps with shock absorption, while also allowing for additional cushioning.”.

Testing footwear is something we’re a little obsessive about, and we’re testing walking shoes on a constant basis. Over the past year alone, we’ve tested over 100 walking shoes, paying attention to fit, comfort, support, and durability. To narrow it down even further, we also consulted podiatrists and certified trainers about their favorite picks.

#18322. Breaking: Walking, Yoga, or Zumba? Which Exercises Help Relieve Menopause Mood Symptoms

📅 17 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (744 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Healthline ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Walking, Yoga, or Zumba? Which Exercises Help Relieve Menopause Mood Symptoms

📅 17 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (744 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Physical activity may help support mood and improve quality of life during the menopause transition, according to a study published on October 13 in Menopause, the journal of the Menopause Society.
  • This review of 12 clinical trials involving over 1,000 people ages 40 to 65 found that both aerobic and mind-body exercises may be associated with reduced depressive symptoms and improved well-being.
  • It is common for individuals to experience psychological symptoms during menopause, including depression, anxiety, low mood, stress, and difficulty with thinking and memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Physical activity may help support mood and improve quality of life during the menopause transition, according to a study published on October 13 in Menopause, the journal of the Menopause Society.

This review of 12 clinical trials involving over 1,000 people ages 40 to 65 found that both aerobic and mind-body exercises may be associated with reduced depressive symptoms and improved well-being.

It is common for individuals to experience psychological symptoms during menopause, including depression, anxiety, low mood, stress, and difficulty with thinking and memory. These symptoms can have a significant effect on quality of life, with an estimated 1 in 10 women leaving work due to menopause symptoms.

This study found that regular physical activity may help improve certain psychological symptoms and overall quality of life during menopause.

The types of physical activity in the review were broken into two categories: aerobic-based exercise (ABIs) and mind-body activities (MBAs).

The researchers found that ABIs showed the strongest effects on reducing depressive symptoms and improving overall quality of life. This may be particularly relevant during perimenopause when women may be more vulnerable to mood instability due to estrogen fluctuations.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, pointed out that there are various ways that ABIs can have positive effects.

Ross explained that aerobic exercise may help improve menopausal symptoms through several mechanisms, including the release of endorphins, reduced inflammation, improved cholesterol levels, and better regulation of body temperature and sleep cycles.

Industry observers note that MBAs were shown to have a greater effect on improving psychological quality of life. These exercises involve mindfulness, body awareness, and breathwork. They may help improve emotional regulation.

ABIs tended to require fewer sessions. This may mean these types of exercises are easier to fit in, especially if you are facing time or energy constraints. For example, in one trial, participants were instructed to walk for 30 minutes, three times per week. In another trial, participants attended three hour-long Zumba classes per week.

In contrast, one trial using MBAs instructed participants to attend two 75-minute yoga classes each week, and another had participants attend daily one-hour yoga classes.

Stephanie Faubion, MD, Director for the Mayo Clinic Center for Women’s Health and Medical Director for The Menopause Society, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings are encouraging.

However, she also cautioned that this was a relatively small body of evidence. “While physical activity is an crucial component of a healthy lifestyle during midlife, I would be cautious about interpreting these findings to mean that exercise is a treatment for depression related specifically to menopause,” she remarked.

It has been revealed that research has shown that physical activity can positively affect mental health. Studies have also found that regular exercise can help improve symptoms of depression and anxiety.

Faubion told Healthline that, broadly speaking, regular physical activity may support mood through multiple pathways, including better sleep, improved physical function, and overall well-being.

However, she also noted that this study cannot tell us precisely why the improvements occurred or whether aerobic exercise is superior to other forms of activity.

Faubion said that recommending physical activity during and after menopause extends well beyond mood.

“Physical activity is important for cardiovascular and metabolic health, maintaining muscle mass and physical function, and supporting bone health,” she said.

“These become particularly vital at midlife as women experience age- and menopause-related changes in body composition, bone, and cardiometabolic health,” Faubion added.

Recent findings suggest that ross agreed that physical activity is important for more than just mood and mental health improvement. She also noted that there are other types of exercise beyond ABIs and MBAs that can benefit people during menopause:.

“These types of activities help with weight loss or allow women to maintain a healthy weight. If you are not ready for aerobic exercises, stretching and simple exercises help with balance and stability,” Ross mentioned.

Faubion told Healthline that physical activity is an vital part of healthy aging and should be encouraged during the menopause transition, but it should not be suggested that women can simply exercise their way out of significant depression or other bothersome menopause symptoms.

“Women experiencing persistent depression, anxiety, or symptoms that interfere with their quality of life should seek evaluation and discuss the full range of evidence-based treatment options with their healthcare clinician,” Faubion mentioned.

In a recent development, A pair of workout leggings is the most notable piece of activewear you’ll buy—but it’s also one of the hardest to get right. Too compressive and they dig in. #18316. Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Increase Dementia, Stroke Risk

Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Increase Dementia, Stroke Risk

📅 18 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (840 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Healthy adults who eat high levels of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may be more likely to show signs of damage to the brain that could increase the likelihood of stroke and future memory problems, according to a study published October 15 in JAMA Network Open.
  • According to recent reports, UPFs are often defined using the NOVA classification: These foods typically have 5 or more ingredients and include substances not typically found in culinary preparations.
  • UPFs account for more than 50% of daily energy intake in high-income countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Healthy adults who eat high levels of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may be more likely to show signs of damage to the brain that could increase the likelihood of stroke and future memory problems, according to a study published October 15 in JAMA Network Open.

According to recent reports, UPFs are often defined using the NOVA classification: These foods typically have 5 or more ingredients and include substances not typically found in culinary preparations. This category of foods includes packaged snack foods, sugary cereals, soft drinks, and frozen ready-to-eat meals.

UPFs account for more than 50% of daily energy intake in high-income countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.

Previous research has linked these foods to adverse cardiometabolic outcomes. This fresh study adds to growing evidence linking high UPF intake to adverse health outcomes.

It has been revealed that this was a cross-sectional analysis of 8,783 adults between the ages of 35 and 69 without cardiovascular disease. The participants were all enrolled in the Canadian Alliance for Healthy Hearts and Minds (CAHHM) and Prospective Urban and Rural Epidemiology-MIND (PURE-MIND) cohorts.

According to recent reports, the researchers used MRI scans to evaluate the participants’ brains. They also set out to analyze the cross-sectional relationship between UPF consumption, body fat, vascular brain injury (VBI), and cognitive performance.

They measured the participants’ habitual UPF intake using a food frequency questionnaire. Intake was expressed as servings based on a 2,000-calorie-per-day diet.

Recent findings suggest that UPFs accounted for an average of 25% of participants’ daily diets. For the individuals with the highest intake, this increased to 45% of everything on their plates, compared to 16% for those who ate the least.

The researchers also noted that UPFs were not just an added part of individual diets. These foods appeared to replace whole foods.

Recent findings suggest that among people with the highest UPF intake, fruits, vegetables, grains, and other minimally processed foods accounted for 41% of their daily food intake. Among those with the lowest UPF intake, minimally processed foods made up 68% of their daily intake.

When the researchers compared the highest intake to the lowest, they found that those with a higher intake of UPFs had 1.7% more body fat. They also found that people with a higher UPF intake had higher odds of VBI.

“These findings are concerning, but it is important to remember that an association does not prove cause and effect,” said Michelle Routhenstein, Preventive Cardiology Dietitian at Entirely Nourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“From my perspective as a preventive cardiology dietitian, these findings reinforce the importance of nourishing our blood vessels to support both cardiovascular and brain health.”.

Although researchers found no significant differences in cognitive performance, the signs of vascular brain injury observed in the study have been associated with an increased risk of stroke and cognitive decline.

These findings suggest a possible link between UPF intake and signs of brain changes. However, participants were only assessed once and weren’t followed over time. This means the researchers were unable to determine whether UPFs directly caused the changes.

“While we can’t conclude from this study that limiting UPFs would improve brain health, we have decades of literature demonstrating that higher intakes of green leafy vegetables, brightly colored fruits, whole grains, and lean protein sources are good for brain health,” remarked Suzanne Judd, PhD, Director of the UC College of Medicine’s Center for Public Health, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“So focusing more on what can be brought into the diet rather than what should be eliminated might be a good way to start,” she added.

The preservatives [in UPFs] may have a direct impact on the vascular system, while the loss of antioxidants results in a less robust response to inflammation in the body.

“Additionally, sugar or salt is often added to make the food a bit tastier so people consume it in higher quantities. Over-consumption of food can lead to weight gain and diabetes, which can negatively impact brain health,” Judd said.

Judd told Healthline that it is virtually impossible to completely avoid UPFs. Even some “health” foods, like protein powder and some yogurts, are considered ultra-processed.

It is more important to look at diet overall and emphasize consuming foods as close to their natural state as possible, such as fruits, vegetables, grains, and meats purchased raw or frozen and then cooked at home.

Routhenstein recommended starting simply with one manageable swap rather than trying to overhaul your entire diet.

She mentioned that you should identify an ultra-processed food you eat regularly and consider a more nutrient-rich alternative. It is important to account for convenience, food preferences, budget, and lifestyle so that the change feels realistic and is sustainable over the long term.

It has been revealed that “I want people to feel empowered, not fearful, when making food choices,” said Routhenstein. “Healthy eating does not mean having to cook everything from scratch. What matters most is building consistent, nourishing habits that support both heart and brain health.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a society, we’re in our protein era, and that’s a good thing. The macronutrient is super key for building and repairing muscles, everyday body functionality, and immune and hormone health. Plus, it helps keep you full.

Since it's so notable, it's also no surprise that you need quite a bit of it, even though pulling that off might get a little tricky sometimes. While the recommended dietary allowance for protein has remained the same for 30 years—at 0.36 grams per pound of total body weight, or 0.8 grams per kilogram—research now suggests that we need more like one gram per pound. (Psst: that higher number is especially important for anyone who regularly hits the gym.) One easy way to make sure you get there? Following high-protein recipes, where all the calculations are already done for you.

According to recent reports, the Women's Health kitchen has you covered. Every single one of the high-protein recipes below packs in at least 20 grams of the macro. These high-protein meals offer a variety of beyond-delicious ways to get more of it into your diet. From high-protein breakfast recipes to steak dinners and meatless options, there's something for everyone. Ready to get cooking?

Experts Warn That a Deadly Disease That Causes ‘Immune Amnesia’ Is Surging in the U.S.

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (678 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that this week, the United States officially lost its measles elimination status, after 26 years.
  • Recent findings suggest that but measles cases have surged in the U.S.
  • In a recent development, doctors fall squarely into the “very concerned” camp for a few reasons.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this week, the United States officially lost its measles elimination status, after 26 years. The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), which oversees measles elimination status, said in a statement on Tuesday that the U.S., along with Bolivia and Mexico, “lost their status after the same measles virus lineage circulated uninterrupted for 12 months or more.”.

Recent findings suggest that but measles cases have surged in the U.S. throughout 2026. The most recent CDC surveillance stats on measles report 5,412 confirmed cases in the country, with 47 states affected. Given that measles hasn’t been a large problem in America for decades, it’s fair to be unsure what to think right now.

In a recent development, doctors fall squarely into the “very concerned” camp for a few reasons. “Measles is not a trivial infection,” indicates William Schaffner, MD, an infectious disease specialist and professor at the Vanderbilt University School of Medicine.

Sources indicate that not only can measles be miserable to experience, but it can also cause lingering effects that can lead to everything from deafness to brain infections, Dr. Schaffner points out. Measles can even cause something known as “immune amnesia,” where your body’s immunity to a range of pathogens is basically wiped out. (More on that in a moment.).

Here’s what infectious disease doctors say:.

Meet the experts: Thomas Russo, MD, professor and chief of infectious disease at the University at Buffalo in Latest York; William Schaffner, MD, an infectious disease specialist and professor at the Vanderbilt University School of Medicine; and Amesh A. Adalja, MD, a senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security.

Recent findings suggest that measles, which is also known as rubeola, is a very contagious viral infection, per the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Measles is so contagious, in fact, that up to 90 percent of people who come into contact with someone with the virus will get it if they’re not protected (like through the vaccine).

Measles usually causes symptoms like a cough, runny nose, tiny spots inside the mouth, a rash, and a high fever. It can also lead to severe complications like pneumonia, immune amnesia, and encephalitis (aka swelling of the brain). “Even with uncomplicated measles, people are usually miserable for a week,” Dr. Schaffner notes.

Measles can also cause “immune amnesia,” meaning the virus can wipe out memory B cells and memory T cells that your immune system has built up from previous infections. “There’s a window after having measles where your immune system has taken a hit, and you have increased susceptibility to viruses, pneumonia, and diarrheal illness—it’s a real thing,” indicates Thomas Russo, MD, professor and chief of infectious disease at the University at Buffalo in Fresh York. This can last for several months, or possibly even longer, he says.

Again, measles was considered eliminated from the U.S. back in 2000, meaning the virus wasn’t considered to be spreading in the U.S. While the country did see some measles cases, they were usually in people who had visited other countries. However, according to the latest CDC stats, only 18 of the 5,412 confirmed cases were from international travelers this year.

Cases began slowly creeping up last year, with CDC data showing 2,289 cases were reported. This trend continued when, this July, a little over the halfway point of the year, there were already 2,318 cases reported. At the time, Amesh A. Adalja, MD, a senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security, noted that this was the highest number of cases seen since the disease was considered eliminated from the country. “Cases were higher only in the early 1990s.”.

According to recent reports, doctors agree that lack of vaccination is the big element behind this increase in cases. “It’s all about vaccination,” Dr. Russo claims. “The anti-vaxx movement is more potent now, and they’re winning.”.

It has been revealed that with fewer parents giving their children the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine, measles cases are creeping back up, Dr. Russo points out.

#18310. A Handful of Pistachios May Help You Sleep Better, Review Claims

📅 19 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1070 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Healthline ↗ Open Full Page

A Handful of Pistachios May Help You Sleep Better, Review Claims

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1070 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Could a handful of pistachios before you go to bed really help you sleep better?
  • A review of studies published in Nutrition Research Reviews examines how the nutrients and plant compounds in pistachios might influence sleep health.
  • Pistachios contain several nutrients linked to sleep-related processes, prompting an investigation into whether they might offer benefits beyond their nutritional value.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Could a handful of pistachios before you go to bed really help you sleep better?

A review of studies published in Nutrition Research Reviews examines how the nutrients and plant compounds in pistachios might influence sleep health.

Pistachios contain several nutrients linked to sleep-related processes, prompting an investigation into whether they might offer benefits beyond their nutritional value.

While the findings suggest that pistachios may support sleep, the evidence is inconclusive and warrants further study.

“Pistachios are compelling for sleep research because they bring together several nutrients and plant compounds connected to sleep physiology within one whole food,” noted study author Marie-Pierre St-Onge, PhD, professor of nutritional medicine and director of the Center of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Research in the Department of Medicine at Columbia University Institute of Nutrition, in a news release.

“Rather than focusing on a single ‘sleep nutrient,’ this review provides a rationale for studying how the complete pistachio food matrix may affect sleep-related pathways,” she continued.

The narrative review examined existing research on pistachios and sleep-related biology.

The researchers explored whether the combination of nutrients in pistachios could promote quality sleep.

Rather than identifying pistachios as a sleep remedy, the researchers outlined biological pathways through which their nutrients and bioactive compounds might influence sleep.

“We were particularly interested in pistachios because they are particularly high in phytomelatonin, polyphenols, and carotenoids, which we noted were plant-derived components that had been shown to have sleep benefits in preclinical studies,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“We also noted their high content of tryptophan and vitamin B6, which are relevant to melatonin production in humans,” she continued.

Pistachios contain several nutrients associated with sleep, including melatonin, which helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle.

Other studies examining the effects of some of these nutrients on sleep offer further context.

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of tryptophan supplementation found that it may reduce wakefulness after sleep onset, particularly at doses of at least 1 gram (g) daily. However, an ounce of pistachios supplies only about 71 mg, which is much less than the doses examined by the researchers.

Additionally, a 2023 review of dietary polyphenols led by St-Onge identified potential links between plant compounds and sleep outcomes, although results varied across studies.

Neither review established that polyphenols or tryptophan from pistachios specifically affected sleep quality.

“I was not surprised that pistachios may help support sleep, given their combination of nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” remarked Michelle Routhenstein, MS, a preventive cardiology dietitian at EntirelyNourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“Pistachios provide tryptophan, an amino acid the body uses to produce serotonin and melatonin; vitamin B6, which supports these pathways; and magnesium, which plays a role in nervous system function and sleep regulation,” she told Healthline.

The newly introduced review highlights the concept of the “food matrix,” or how nutrients and bioactive compounds interact within a whole food.

Instead of investigating tryptophan, magnesium, or melatonin individually, researchers were curious about the combined effects of consuming them together in pistachios.

It has been revealed that laboratory and simulated-digestion research offers clues about how fiber and plant compounds in pistachios and peanuts interact with gut microbes. However, these findings do not establish that eating pistachios changes sleep quality in real-world conditions.

Broader nutrition research also points to a relationship between diet and sleep.

A 2021 review in the Annual Review of Nutrition examined evidence linking dietary patterns and individual nutrients to sleep outcomes. The findings suggest a relationship between sleep and diet, but note that more research is needed to determine cause and effect.

In a nutshell, the current evidence builds a compelling case for pistachios as a sleep aid.

However, it’s too soon to recommend pistachios as a sleep remedy, as many factors may affect sleep quality and insomnia.

In a recent development, “Sleep difficulties can have different underlying causes,” Routhenstein noted. “If inadequate intake of these nutrients is a contributing factor, pistachios may help, but they may not address sleep issues related to other nutrient deficiencies or other causes.”.

Much of the supporting evidence cited in the review comes from studies of individual nutrients, other foods, laboratory experiments, or biological mechanisms rather than from trials involving whole pistachios.

Researchers have also reported significant variations in the melatonin content of pistachios, making the amount in a typical serving difficult to pinpoint.

Additionally, the review received support from American Pistachio Growers, and the corresponding author, St-Onge, serves on its advisory board. Larger studies and clinical trials are needed, ideally without industry funding, to ensure well-rounded results.

Indeed, the authors call for randomized controlled trials examining whether eating pistachios affects sleep outcomes, including sleep quality, duration, and melatonin levels.

“This was a review; we noted that the complete profile of pistachios would make them well-suited to support healthful sleep, but research is needed to evaluate this,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“This is the next step, and something we are actively working on. We also need to better understand what dosage and frequency of consumption would be optimal.”.

Regardless, a handful of pistachios is still considered a healthy choice as part of a balanced diet.

“A small handful, about 1 ounce of shelled pistachios, is an appropriate portion,” Routhenstein said. “Enjoy them during the day or as a light afternoon or evening snack when you’re hungry.”.

If nutrients like tryptophan help promote sleep, it’s possible that other nuts could yield similar results.

“Other nuts, such as almonds and walnuts, may offer similar benefits because they also contain nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” Routhenstein said.

“Early research is encouraging, but it’s too soon to say how much they might help.”.

Other foods, like turkey, also contain tryptophan.

“For someone allergic to nuts, foods such as tofu, beans, oats, eggs, dairy, and fish can provide tryptophan, which the body uses to make serotonin and melatonin,” Routhenstein said. “The goal is to meet their nutrient needs rather than rely on one food to improve sleep.”.

Recent findings suggest that sleep health depends on multiple factors. As such, Routhenstein recommends a personalized approach to getting better sleep, from what you eat and when you eat to addressing any nutritional gaps.

“I would also encourage regular, balanced meals throughout the day to support blood sugar management, especially for those with diabetes, while avoiding large meals close to bedtime,” Routhenstein mentioned. “Caffeine later in the day and alcohol in the evening are also worth considering as possible sleep disruptors.”.

BYD’s newly introduced flagship Tang SUV starts at about $34,000 with two enormous screens

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (637 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, BYD opened pre-orders for the third-generation Tang starting at about $34,000 in China.
  • The third-generation Tang joins the Great Tang, or Da Tang, as it’s called in China in BYD’s expanding flagship SUV lineup.
  • We knew it was coming soon after the upcoming model appeared in a regulatory filing in China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) last month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, BYD opened pre-orders for the third-generation Tang starting at about $34,000 in China. This five-seat flagship SUV packs more than you’d expect for the money, with two massive 30-inch-plus screens inside and up to 850 km (528 miles) of CLTC range.

The third-generation Tang joins the Great Tang, or Da Tang, as it’s called in China in BYD’s expanding flagship SUV lineup.

We knew it was coming soon after the upcoming model appeared in a regulatory filing in China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) last month.

BYD announced on Friday that pre-orders for the third-gen Tang are officially open, starting at 225,000 yuan, which is around $34,000.

The “large five-seat flagship SUV,” as BYD calls it, is available in three variants, priced from 225,000 yuan ($34,000), 240,000 yuan ($36,000), and 260,000 yuan ($39,000) with rear- and all-wheel-drive variants.

The two lower-priced variants are both RWD, offering a CLTC range of up to 850 km (528 miles), while the top-spec dual-motor AWD version has up to 770 km (478 miles).

All versions use BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging tech, enabling the battery to be charged from 10% to 80% in five minutes, or nine minutes to go from 10% to 97%.

Inside, the five-seat SUV packs a surprising amount of tech and premium extras for the price. The setup features two massive screens: a 35.4″ integrated display and another 30″ panoramic theater screen.

Unlike its predessor, which offered five and six-seat configurations, the third-gen Tang will only be offered as a five-seater.

The five-seat setup opens up interior space for passengers and the third-gen Tang has the largest front trunk (frunk) in its class at 205L, BYD said.

Like many of its latest flagship vehicles, the third-gen Tang is equipped with BYD’s latest tech, including its God’s Eye B driver-assistance system and Disus-A dual-chamber intelligent air suspension body control system.

Other added features include a 22-speaker Dynaudio sound system, intelligent electric all‑wheel drive, a high-speed tire blowout stability system, and its iTAC intelligent torque control system.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, formally known as cultivated meat, lab-grown meat has been in development for more than a decade, but it’s only recently begun to capture mainstream attention.
  • Meet the experts: Elliot Swartz, PhD, is a cultivated meat researcher and the senior principal scientist for cultivated meat at The Good Food Institute.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that lab-grown meat is having an absolute field day on social media, as tons of outlandish claims and conspiracy theories about it are forming: The lab-grown industry is trying to sneak it into our grocery carts by labeling it as natural meat! Here’s why you need to avoid it at all costs! In truth, there’s a lot more to the story, and a ton of those claims are false.

According to recent reports, formally known as cultivated meat, lab-grown meat has been in development for more than a decade, but it’s only recently begun to capture mainstream attention. In 2023, it received regulatory clearance from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA). Now, it’s beginning to make its way into the market (albeit in limited quantities), indicates Steven Surico, RD, a registered dietitian with the Food and Nutrition Department at Good Samaritan University Hospital.

Meet the experts: Elliot Swartz, PhD, is a cultivated meat researcher and the senior principal scientist for cultivated meat at The Good Food Institute. Steven Surico, RD, is a registered dietitian with the Food and Nutrition Department at Good Samaritan University Hospital. Lauri Wright, RDN, is a registered dietitian and associate professor of nutrition and dietetics at the University of South Florida College of Public Health.

According to recent reports, as such, lab-grown meat is becoming a grossly misunderstood concept. (Cue: The recent influx of misleading social media videos and AI-generated content.) These posts can blur the line between fact and fiction, leaving consumers unsure of what’s real, scaring them when there’s nothing to be afraid of. “The concern is that cultivated meat is something highly artificial, when in reality, it’s not,” claims Surico.

Here’s everything you need to know about lab-grown meat, including what it is, whether it’s being sold in stores, and if you should truly worry about it, according to experts.

Cultivated meat is grown directly from animal cells, as opposed to natural meat that’s produced by raising and slaughtering an animal, claims Elliot Swartz, PhD, a cultivated meat researcher and the senior principal scientist for cultivated meat at The Good Food Institute.

Sources indicate that “A small sample of cells is fed basic nutrients, like amino acids, fats, vitamins, salts, and sugars, in clean, controlled environments similar to those used to make yogurt, cheese, and beer, where the cells are grown and developed into meat or seafood,” he explains. As the cells multiply and develop, they form the muscle and other tissues that make up meat. Once mature, Swartz says they’re harvested and prepared as a product that should, at least in theory, offer the same taste, smell, texture, and consistency as ordinary meat.

It has been revealed that lab-grown meat vs. plant-based alternatives: “Beyond Meat products are made primarily from plant ingredients and do not contain animal muscle cells, whereas cultivated meat starts with animal cells and grows those cells into animal tissue,” Surico says.

Industry observers note that cultivated meat may address some of the challenges associated with natural meat production, particularly when it comes to food safety, public health, nutrition, and the environmental impact of raising livestock. According to Swartz, one of the biggest advantages is the greater control over the production process, which could offer significant food safety benefits.

According to recent reports, research shows that raising large populations of animals in close quarters can create opportunities for bacteria, other pathogens, and diseases to spread. This can increase the risk of transmission to humans through food (or animal) contact, but cultivated meat could help reduce these risks, Swartz explains.

Cultivated meat is also better for the environment by reducing the land, water, and greenhouse gas emissions needed for meat production. Research from The Good Food Institute even suggests that if cultivated meat can be produced commercially in large quantities using clean energy, it could have a significantly smaller environmental footprint than conventional meat.

Finally, because the cells are grown in a controlled environment, researchers can influence the nutritional composition of the meat, says Lauri Wright, RDN, a registered dietitian and associate professor of nutrition and dietetics at the University of South Florida College of Public Health. For example, they can adjust the amount and types of fat in the meat to reduce saturated fat and cholesterol while increasing desirable nutrients like protein, she explains. Theoretically, this could lead to healthier meat that tastes the same, studies suggest.

Sources indicate that while some people are afraid of lab-grown meat because they’re not really sure what’s in it, each product undergoes extensive testing by the FDA and USDA. So, its nutritional content is thoroughly tested to ensure it meets food safety standards, adds Swartz.

Sources indicate that yes, but availability is extremely limited. Cultivated meat has received approval from the FDA and USDA for sale in the U.S., as well as in Singapore and Australia, per The Good Food Institute. However, regulatory approval doesn’t necessarily mean that products are widely available. Plus, eight states in the U.S. have enacted bans or temporary restrictions on cultivated meat, including Alabama, Florida, Indiana, Mississippi, Montana, South Dakota, Nebraska, and Texas. These restrictions are largely driven by concerns about protecting traditional agriculture and livestock industries.

Sources indicate that so, contrary to what social media might have you believing, cultivated meat isn’t something you can pick up at your local supermarket just yet. In the U.S., the only product presently being served is Wildtype’s cultivated salmon, which is available at a handful of select restaurants in Washington D.C., Oregon, Arizona, and California.

In a recent development, while it’s difficult to predict exactly when lab-grown meat will be in grocery stores, Swartz expects a gradual rollout, with smaller, more specialized retailers being the first to carry it. “You could start to see cultivated meat products more widely introduced in higher-end retailers in the early 2030s, but I don’t think you’ll see it in big box grocery stores until the late 2030s,” he notes.

In grocery stores, it’ll be clearly labeled as lab-grown or cultivated meat. “Due to the USDA regulations and labeling, it should be very clear to the consumer if they are buying regular meat or lab-grown meat,” notes Surico. In fact, federal law prohibits food from being misbranded or carrying false or misleading labels, and regulators have stated cultivated meat products must be clearly and accurately labeled.

According to recent reports, as for the price, that remains to be seen. Cultivated meat is at the moment more expensive to produce than most conventional meat and seafood, but Swartz claims the long-term goal is to bring production costs down to match or fall below those of conventional options.

It has been revealed that not very. “You should not be freaked out,” states Wright. “If anything, you should see it as potential, because the future of lab-grown meat could give consumers more options and alternatives to what they buy and put into their body.”.

It has been revealed that swartz agrees, pointing out that the benefits go beyond offering another way to produce meat. “Whether you care about the environment, animal welfare, food safety, or public health, there’s a lot of potential benefits for cultivated meat that are additive in terms of value for the consumer,” he says.

Industry observers note that of course, that doesn’t mean everyone has to embrace cultivated meat—traditional meat isn’t going away or being phased out of grocery stores or restaurants. The goal is simply to give consumers another option, not replace the foods they already know and enjoy. And if cultivated meat isn’t your jam, that’s perfectly fine, too.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • An “exceptionally rare” yellow-colored burbot (Lota lota) was recently caught by a team of U.S.
  • Burbots are long fish that weigh about three to five pounds on average, and live in cold rivers and lakes of North America, Europe, and Asia.
  • The team caught the brightly colored fish during a routine aquatic invasive species survey.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We’ll call him mellow yellow. An “exceptionally rare” yellow-colored burbot (Lota lota) was recently caught by a team of U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) biologists in Oswego Harbor on Lake Ontario in Upstate Newly introduced York.

Burbots are long fish that weigh about three to five pounds on average, and live in cold rivers and lakes of North America, Europe, and Asia. To the naked eye, they appear scaleless, but are actually covered with tiny, almost microscopic scales. What they eat depends on their size. Smaller burbots will eat zooplankton, while bigger burbots prefer to snack on other fish.

The team caught the brightly colored fish during a routine aquatic invasive species survey. It gets its unique color from a rare genetic condition called xanthochromism. A genetic mutation suppresses the normal pigmentation, it produces a yellow-orange appearance instead of the burbot’s usual grey, olive, or tan coloring. In wild fish, xanthochromism is less common than albinism or melanism, making this fish an “especially unusual capture.”.

According to recent reports, the burbot is a native species in the Great Lakes, but the USFWS team says the discovery highlights the effectiveness of the Service’s Aquatic Invasive Species Early Detection and Monitoring Program. The program uses a multi-gear fish-surveillance strategy to detect certain non-native species in the harbors, rivers, and embayments of the Great Lakes. Early detection of a watchlist species gives fisheries managers the best opportunity to implement prevention and removal measures if invasive species are detected. Since invasive species are often rare when they first enter fresh waters, the program uses electrofishing, fyke-netting, gill-netting, and environmental DNA (eDNA) analysis to increase the chances that scientists detect an invasive species.

“The finding is notable because burbot populations in the lake are extremely low, and the species typically inhabit deeper, cooler waters than those found within the harbor,” the USFWS wrote in a statement. “It represents the first documented detection of a burbot during a fisheries survey in Oswego Harbor, although a few angler catches have been reported.”.

It has been revealed that the United States Geological Survey (USGS) fisheries biologists, who examined the fish and are familiar with the species, also observed that it was very thin and appeared to be in poor health. It was later sent to the Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine for a health analysis due to the “unexplained factors contributing to the continued suppression of its population”.

“The discovery could turn out to be lucky for the burbot too; this exceptionally rare fish may provide valuable insight into the health of the species’ populations throughout the basin that can inform management actions,” the USFWS concluded.
